Mecca (UNA/SPA) - The Ministerial Council of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) affirmed the support of the Gulf states for the brotherly Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip and its surroundings, the lifting of the blockade imposed on the Gaza Strip, the alleviation of the suffering of the Palestinian people and the securing of the delivery of humanitarian and rapid assistance to the residents of Gaza, calling for the protection of the civilian population, refraining from targeting them, and for compliance with and adherence to international law and international humanitarian law without exception.

The Ministerial Council positively assessed the outcomes of the extraordinary Arab summit, the "Palestine Summit", held on 4 March in Cairo to discuss the serious developments in the Palestinian question of late, emphasising what was said in the summit's statement.

This was stated in the final communique issued at the 163rd session of the Gulf Cooperation Council, held in Mecca.

The Ministerial Council of the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf held its session on Thursday, 6 Ramadan 1446 AH, corresponding to March 2025, with the participation of His Highness Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the United Arab Emirates; His Excellency Dr. Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Bahrain; His Highness Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia; His Excellency Sayyid Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Sultanate of Oman; and His Excellency Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the State of Qatar.

The meeting was attended by His Excellency the Secretary-General of the Gulf Cooperation Council, Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi.

The Ministerial Council highly appreciated the outcomes of the extraordinary summit of Arab countries, the "Palestine Summit", held on 4 March 2025 in Cairo, Arab Republic of Egypt, to discuss the grave developments witnessed of late in the Palestinian question, emphasising what was said in the statement issued at the summit.

The Ministerial Council congratulated the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, His Royal Highness Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crown Prince and Prime Minister, and the people of Saudi Arabia on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's victory in winning the right to host the 2034 FIFA World Cup.

The Ministerial Council also congratulated His Highness Sheikh Meshal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah, Emir of the State of Kuwait, on the successful hosting of the 26th Gulf Cup football championship, congratulated the Kingdom of Bahrain on winning the championship trophy, and extended sincere congratulations and wishes for further progress and success to the people of the State of Kuwait.

The Ministerial Council highly appreciated the success of the UAE in holding the new editions of IDEX and NAVDEX from 17 to 21 February 2025, as they provided an exceptional platform for showcasing the latest innovative solutions in 17 key sectors, including vehicles and land systems, aircraft and air systems, and unmanned systems, reflecting progress in smart mobility technologies and autonomous operations, and highlighting new innovations and technologies in the field of defence and security, including land, air, sea and space.

The Ministerial Council also highly appreciated the success of the United Arab Emirates in holding, on 10-12 February 2025, the 2025 "Global Implementation Support Symposium" organised by the General Civil Aviation Authority and the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), along with the accompanying exhibition, in addition to the launch of the first edition of the "Global Sustainable Aviation Market" initiative.

The Ministerial Council of the United Arab Emirates congratulated the 12th World Government Summit, held in Dubai on 10-13 February 2025, and the themes presented there: effective governance, the global economy and financing the future, the sustainability of cities and confronting crises and climate, the future of humanity and capacity development, global transformations in the field of health care, and future prospects of new trends such as artificial intelligence and technology oriented towards sustainable development, as well as the advancement of government work and the strengthening of cooperation between governments.

The Ministerial Council also congratulated the Kingdom of Bahrain on its success in organising the 20th Regional Security Forum, the Manama Dialogue, to discuss important issues on the regional and international stage and to work on proposing effective solutions to them.

The Ministerial Council highly appreciated the success of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in organising the (19th) session of the Global Internet Governance Forum (IGF) to discuss policy issues related to internet governance, to exchange experience, information and best practices, and to identify emerging digital challenges and find solutions to them; to promote international cooperation and raise awareness.

The Ministerial Council welcomed the adoption by the World Intellectual Property Organization of the "Riyadh Design Law Treaty", which will help open new horizons of international cooperation and create legal frameworks that support innovation and creativity worldwide.

The Ministerial Council highly appreciated the success of the Sultanate of Oman in holding the 16th Indian Ocean Conference in Muscat on 17 February 2025 under the motto "A Journey to New Horizons of Maritime Partnership".

The Ministerial Council also highly appreciated the success of the State of Qatar in organising the 2024 Doha Forum under the slogan "The Inevitability of Innovation" on 7 December 2024 and in providing a global platform for innovative discussions on the most important issues and problems worldwide.

The Ministerial Council welcomed the holding by the State of Kuwait on 4 December 2024 of the Global Humanitarian Overview, to be organised by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) under the title "Strengthening Global Solidarity and Empowering Local Communities", highly appreciating the efforts of the State of Kuwait in multilateral international action and its commitment to advancing humanitarian issues and expanding international cooperation amid growing humanitarian challenges.

The Ministerial Council expressed sincere condolences to the victims of the earthquake in the People's Republic of China, the two air disasters in the Republic of Korea and the Republic of Kazakhstan, the forest fires in the state of California in the United States of America, and the hotel fire in Bolu province in the Republic of Turkey, noting the position of solidarity and the official and popular support for the victims and those affected, stemming from their great and expanded role in humanitarian and relief assistance.

The Ministerial Council reviewed the latest developments in joint Gulf action and developments in political issues at the regional and international level as follows:

Joint Gulf action:

1. The Ministerial Council reviewed the results of consultations on the implementation of the decision of the Ministerial Council at its thirty-third session regarding the proposal of the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, may he be pardoned, to move from the stage of cooperation to the stage of union, and instructed the Ministerial Council to continue efforts to move from the stage of cooperation to the stage of union, and also assigned the Ministerial Council and the head of the specialised body to complete the taking of the measures necessary for this and to present what has been achieved to the Ministerial Council at its next session.

2. The Ministerial Council affirmed its interest in the strength and cohesion of the Cooperation Council, the unity of its members and the achievement of greater coordination, integration and interconnection in all fields in order to achieve the aspirations of the citizens of the Council's countries, stressing that its countries stand together in the face of any threat to any of the Council's countries.

The situation in Gaza:

3. The Ministerial Council affirmed the GCC's support for the brotherly Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip and its surroundings, the lifting of the blockade imposed on the Strip, the alleviation of the suffering of the Palestinian people and the provision of all humanitarian and emergency assistance and basic needs to the residents of Gaza. A call for the protection of civilians, for refraining from attacks on them, and for observing and upholding international law and international humanitarian law without exception.

4. The Ministerial Council affirmed the GCC's support for the steadfastness of the Palestinian people on their land and its rejection of any attempts to displace the residents of the Gaza Strip, considering this an outrageous violation of international law and international humanitarian law, and calling for international protection to be provided for the Palestinian people.

5. The Ministerial Council condemned the decision of the Israeli occupation government of 2 March 2025 to halt the entry of humanitarian aid into the Gaza Strip, in serious violation of the ceasefire agreement, international humanitarian law and the Fourth Geneva Convention, and called on the international community to stop these serious Israeli violations, to activate international accountability mechanisms and to ensure sustainable access to aid.

6. The Ministerial Council expressed its condemnation and denunciation of the statements made by Israeli officials regarding the displacement of Palestinians from Gaza, which grossly violates the norms of international law and the Charter of the United Nations.

7. The Ministerial Council highly appreciated the efforts made by the State of Qatar, the Arab Republic of Egypt and the United States of America to reach a ceasefire agreement in the Gaza Strip, stressing the need to adhere to the agreement, to stop Israeli aggression in the Gaza Strip and to withdraw completely from the Strip and all other Palestinian territories, expressing the hope that this agreement will contribute to a permanent ceasefire and allow humanitarian aid to be delivered to them without delay and on a permanent basis. And calling on the international community to pressure Israel to fulfil its obligations in this regard.

8. The Ministerial Council welcomed the joint statement of the Arab six-party meeting in Cairo on Palestine of 1 February 2025, which stressed the importance of maintaining the ceasefire, ensuring the delivery of humanitarian aid to all parts of the Gaza Strip, as well as full support for the steadfastness of the Palestinian people on their land and their preservation of their legitimate rights in accordance with international law, and the rejection of any violations of these inalienable rights through settlement activity, expulsion and demolition of homes, or annexation of land, or through the evacuation of that land of its owners by resettlement or by encouraging the displacement or uprooting of Palestinians from their land by any means, under any circumstances and justifications.

9. The Ministerial Council affirmed Security Council resolutions 2735, 2712 and 2720 regarding the ceasefire in the Gaza Strip, the release of hostages and the exchange of prisoners, the return of civilians to their homes, the safe and effective distribution of humanitarian aid on a large scale, and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Strip. It welcomed the UN General Assembly resolution of 5 December 2024 on a ceasefire in Gaza and on allowing the civilian population in the Gaza Strip to receive basic services and humanitarian aid without hindrance, as well as the need to comply with international law and international humanitarian law and to protect civilians.

10. The Ministerial Council stressed that Israel bears full responsibility for its violations and attacks on the Gaza Strip, which have led to the deaths of tens of thousands of civilians, the majority of them women and children, and considers them war crimes and crimes against humanity under international humanitarian law.

11. The Ministerial Council called on the international community to take the necessary measures within the framework of international law to respond to the practices of the Israeli government and its policy of collective punishment against the residents of the Gaza Strip.

12. The Ministerial Council condemned in the strongest terms the crimes committed by the Israeli occupation forces in the Gaza Strip, in the context of crimes of genocide and ethnic cleansing, including the killing of civilians, torture, execution, disappearances, forced displacement and looting, calling on the Security Council to form an independent international committee to investigate these crimes, to take serious measures to prevent these crimes and to detain their perpetrators, and to provide international protection for the Palestinian people.

13. The Ministerial Council condemned the destruction by the Israeli armed forces of residential areas, hospitals, schools, universities, mosques, churches and infrastructure in the Gaza Strip, including the massacre committed by the Israeli occupation forces in the Nuseirat camp on 13 December 2024, and the burning of the Kamal Adwan Hospital in the Gaza Strip on 27 December 2024 and the subsequent evacuation of all patients and medical staff.

14. The Ministerial Council condemned the attacks by the Israeli occupation forces on humanitarian and international organisations in the Gaza Strip and the attacks by Israeli settlers on humanitarian aid convoys, stressing the responsibility of the Israeli occupation forces to protect these convoys in accordance with international humanitarian law, to deliver the necessary humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip and not to obstruct the work of international organisations.

15. The Ministerial Council affirmed its support for the Palestinian-Egyptian-Arab plan approved by the extraordinary Arab summit, the "Palestine Summit", held on 4 March 2025 in Cairo, Arab Republic of Egypt, stressing that the future of the Gaza Strip must be in the context of a single Palestinian state and the implementation of the two-state solution. The Council also welcomed the summit's decision to hold an international conference on recovery and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip and called on the international community and all brotherly and friendly countries to participate actively and generously in the reconstruction donors' conference, which is planned to be held at the earliest opportunity, and to mobilise the necessary resources to implement the plan in cooperation with the Government of Palestine and the relevant international parties, stressing the importance of strengthening the steadfastness of the Palestinian people, increasing their resilience on their land and involving them in the reconstruction efforts.

16. The Ministerial Council stressed the need to open all crossing points to allow humanitarian aid to enter the Gaza Strip, and to ensure access for any investigation or fact-finding committee regarding the accusation of genocide, stressing the importance of international resolutions covering all the Palestinian territories, in accordance with the relevant resolutions of international legitimacy, and renewing its call on the international community to assume its responsibility to stop the Israeli aggression.

17. The Ministerial Council called on the Security Council to adopt a binding resolution under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations, ensuring the Israeli occupation forces' adherence to a permanent ceasefire, an end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and their forced displacement, the entry of humanitarian aid and a return to normal life in the Gaza Strip.

18. The Ministerial Council welcomed the outcomes of the Ministerial Conference on Strengthening the Humanitarian Response in the Gaza Strip, held in the Arab Republic of Egypt on 2 December 2024, which stressed the need to strengthen the humanitarian response immediately and effectively in order to meet the basic needs of the population in the Gaza Strip and to alleviate the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza.

19. The Ministerial Council noted the efforts made by the GCC countries and the Arab countries at the political level to stop the Israeli attacks on the Gaza Strip, the humanitarian aid and assistance provided by the GCC countries to the Gaza Strip, and the popular campaigns to provide assistance to the Palestinian people and deliver humanitarian aid to the besieged residents.

20. The Ministerial Council stressed the importance of what was said in the statement of the extraordinary Arab summit, the "Palestine Summit", regarding the call to establish an international fund for the care of the orphans of Gaza in cooperation with the United Nations.

The Palestinian cause:

21. The Ministerial Council stressed the central role of the Palestinian cause, the end of the Israeli occupation, and support for the sovereignty of the Palestinian people over all the occupied Palestinian territories. The Council called on all countries to complete their procedures for recognising the State of Palestine and to take immediate collective measures to achieve a permanent solution that guarantees the establishment of an independent Palestinian state on the 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with the Arab Peace Initiative and the resolutions of international legitimacy, stressing the need to intensify cooperation with international and regional powers, as well as to redouble the efforts of the international community to settle the conflict in a manner that meets all the legitimate rights of the brotherly Palestinian people.

22. The Ministerial Council stressed the importance of the initiatives announced by His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, at the Arab Summit held in the Kingdom of Bahrain, calling for an international peace conference in the Middle East to establish a national, independent, secure and sovereign Palestinian State, as well as to support efforts to recognise the Palestinian State internationally and to accept its full membership in the United Nations. The Council also stressed the summit's call for the deployment of international protection and peacekeeping forces linked to the United Nations in the occupied Palestinian territory until the two-state solution is implemented.

23. The Ministerial Council welcomed the recognition by 146 countries so far of the State of Palestine and its sovereignty over its land, highly appreciating the leading role of the Kingdom of Spain in this area, and called on all countries to take the necessary measures to recognise the State of Palestine and to support the national rights of the Palestinian people.

24. The Ministerial Council stressed the importance of what was said in the statement of the extraordinary Arab summit, the "Palestine Summit", regarding the deployment of international protection and peacekeeping forces in the Palestinian territories of Gaza and the West Bank, by decision of the Security Council.

25. The Ministerial Council affirmed its support for the efforts of the international coalition to implement the two-state solution and for the efforts of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, in partnership with the Kingdom of Norway and the European Union, to define a timetable for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and the end of the Israeli occupation, on 15 February 2025, and called on all countries desiring peace to join this initiative.

26. The Ministerial Council welcomed the decision of the United Nations General Assembly to hold a high-level international conference to achieve a peaceful settlement of the Palestinian question and to implement the two-state solution, planned to be held at United Nations Headquarters in New York in June 2025 under the chairmanship of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and France, stressing the importance of active participation in this conference and supporting what the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is doing in this regard.

27. The Ministerial Council affirmed its support for the efforts of the Ministerial Committee chaired by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, which was established by the extraordinary joint Arab and Islamic summit to stop the Israeli aggression against the Palestinian people and to explain the recovery and reconstruction plan in Gaza. It also stressed the importance of the Arab Ministerial Committee in support of the State of Palestine, chaired by the Kingdom of Bahrain, continuing its work and its movement at the international level to support the efforts of the State of Palestine to obtain wider recognition, to gain full membership in the United Nations, to hold an international peace conference and to provide international protection for the Palestinian people.

28. The Ministerial Council affirmed its support for the Conference of the High Contracting Parties to the Geneva Conventions of 1949, to be held in Switzerland on 7 March 2025 to discuss the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territories.

29. The Ministerial Council welcomed the decision of the United Nations General Assembly of 12 December 2024 to request an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice regarding Israel's decision to ban the Agency's work in the occupied territories. Stressing the importance of supporting the agency in light of the critical humanitarian circumstances and its principal role in supporting the relief, humanitarian and development efforts for the Palestinian people.

30. The Ministerial Council welcomed the decision of the United Nations General Assembly of 5 December 2024, in which the Assembly affirmed its full support for the mandate of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) in all areas of its activity, for all the losses, damage and destruction inflicted on the Agency in the occupied Palestinian territories.

31. The Ministerial Council condemned the decision of the Government of Israel of 28 January 2025 to halt the work of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), calling on the United Nations to fulfil its obligations under international law, to oblige the occupying state to revoke this decision and to ensure the continuation of the agency's activity in providing services to Palestinian refugees.

32. The Ministerial Council welcomed the appointment of the Dutch minister Sigrid Kaag as Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, within the framework of the United Nations' ongoing efforts to enhance its role in achieving a just and lasting peace in the Middle East.

33. The Ministerial Council highly appreciated the efforts made by the Arab countries to achieve national reconciliation in order to restore Palestinian national unity, to reunite the Palestinian people and to achieve the interests of the Palestinian people.

34. The Ministerial Council highly appreciated the resolution of the United Nations General Assembly of 13 September 2024 on "ending the unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territories" and on Palestine's right to full membership in the United Nations, calling on the Security Council to issue a resolution swiftly so that the State of Palestine obtains full membership in the United Nations.

35. The Ministerial Council called on the international community to intervene to stop the attacks on the Palestinian presence in the city of Jerusalem, the expulsion of Palestinians from their homes, the attempts to change its legal and historical character, its demographic composition and the arrangements for the Islamic holy sites, as well as the attempts to impose Israeli sovereignty over it in clear violation of international law, international resolutions and the existing agreements concluded in this regard, stressing its rejection of these unilateral measures.

36. The Ministerial Council condemned the continued construction of settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories and the expulsion of Palestinians from their homes, and expressed its rejection of any steps to annex settlements in the West Bank to Israel, which clearly violates the Charter of the United Nations, the principles of international law and United Nations resolutions, including Security Council Resolution 2334 of 2016, the 2004 Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice and the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. The Council called on the international community to pressure the Israeli authorities to revoke the settlement decisions that violate international laws and resolutions.

37. The Ministerial Council condemned the accusations and claims of the Israeli occupation regarding a published map showing parts of Arab countries (Jordan, Lebanon, Syria) within its borders, warning that the publication of such maps would harm the chances of peace in the region.

38. The Ministerial Council condemned the continuing attacks of the Israeli occupation in the West Bank, including the bombardment of the city of Tammun on 29 January 2025 and the bombardment of the city of Jenin on 23 January 2025 and its systematic destruction of infrastructure, calling on the international community to make efforts to prevent further loss of life and to avoid further strangulation in the Palestinian territory.

39. The Ministerial Council highly appreciated the decision of the Executive Board of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) of 16 October 2024, which called on the Israeli occupation government, as the occupying power, to cease all its unilateral measures aimed at changing the historical and legal status quo in Jerusalem and its holy sites, and to consider them null and void.

40. The Ministerial Council condemned the storming of the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque by the Israeli Minister of National Security under the protection of the occupation authorities on 26 December 2024, in violation of Security Council resolutions, especially Resolution No. 2334. It also condemned the repeated storming of the courtyards of the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque by settlers and Israeli officials, in serious violation of international law and of the historical and legal status quo in Jerusalem and its holy sites, as well as the violation of the sanctity of the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque and the provocation of the feelings of Muslims, stressing that the continuing violations and attacks on the holy sites aggravate tensions and push the situation towards an unending cycle of violence.

The Iranian occupation of the three United Arab Emirates islands:

41. The Ministerial Council affirmed its firm position and previous decisions regarding the condemnation of Iran's continued occupation of the three islands (Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa) belonging to the United Arab Emirates, affirming the following:

1. Supporting the UAE's right to sovereignty over the three islands, Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa, as well as over the territorial waters, airspace, continental shelf and exclusive economic zone of the three islands, considering them an integral part of the territory of the UAE.

2. Considering that any decisions, practices or actions carried out by Iran on the three islands are null and void and change nothing of the historical and legal facts unanimously agreed regarding the United Arab Emirates' right of sovereignty over its three islands.

3. Calling on Iran to respond to the UAE's efforts to resolve the issue through direct negotiations or recourse to the International Court of Justice.

42. The Ministerial Council condemned the continued construction of housing by the Government of Iran to settle Iranians on the three islands occupied by Iran, as well as the escalation of positions and measures taken by the Iranian authorities, including the statements of the Iranian Deputy Minister of Roads and Urban Development Arsalan Maleki on 12 May 2024 regarding Iran's intention to grant illegal land and housing projects on the occupied island of Abu Musa, and the statements of the (late) President of Iran on 4 February 2024 during a cabinet session about Iranian industrial efforts on the islands, in addition to the statements of Mohammad Mokhber, First Vice-President of Iran, on 11 January 2024 regarding the completion of what he called the Document on the Development of the Three Islands, and what this includes in terms of the construction of housing and projects on the three UAE islands.

43. The Ministerial Council condemned the Government of Iran's continued construction of illegal colonial housing to settle Iranians on the three Emirati islands occupied by Iran, and the escalation of the positions and measures taken by the Iranian authorities, including the announcement by Ali Akbar Safaei, Deputy Minister of Roads and Urban Development, on 5 November 2024 of the start of construction of 110 housing units on the island of Abu Musa and the opening of the multi-purpose port of Abu Musa.

44. The Ministerial Council condemned the Iranian military manoeuvres that included the three occupied islands of the United Arab Emirates, Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa, as well as the territorial waters, airspace, continental shelf and exclusive economic zone of the three islands as an integral part of the territory of the United Arab Emirates, the latest of which were the Iranian military manoeuvres and the holding of combat exercises on the occupied island of Abu Musa on 20 June 2024. It called on Iran to stop such violations and provocative actions, which constitute interference in the internal affairs of an independent, sovereign state, do not contribute to building confidence, threaten security and stability in the region and endanger the safety and security of regional and international navigation in the Gulf.

45. The Ministerial Council condemned the repeated visits of senior Iranian officials to the three occupied UAE islands of Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa, the latest of which was the visit of Mohammad Haq Shenas, Assistant Minister of Cultural Heritage of Iran, and Hadi Moin Far, Deputy Director for Tourism at the General Directorate of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts in Hormozgan province, on 24 January 2024 to tourism and handicraft projects and opportunities on the island of Abu Musa, occupied by Iran; Ali Ozmai, commander of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Navy, and Major General Ali Reza Tansiri, commander of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Navy, also visited the Iranian-occupied island of Abu Musa on 12 January 2025 at the head of a delegation of the Iranian National Defence University, which included students from brotherly and friendly countries.

The Durra field:

46. a3335.t:
The Ombetja Yehinga Organisation (OYO) has reduced its social outreach projects due to USAID funding cuts implemented by the US government earlier this year.
OYO, a non-governmental organisation, focuses on youth education and development through art and works with subcontracted institutions that are USAID-funded.
When the funding was abruptly suspended, the impact was felt immediately.
"When the funding from those partners was suspended, it obviously affected us because we are sub-recipients and rely on that money. So it did affect us. And unfortunately, this year, we could only do fewer projects than we normally do. And we could reach many fewer regions than we normally do," said OYO Director Philippe Talavera.
The organisation, which relies on donor funding, had to find ways to stay afloat and continue advocating for social change.
Of late, the French Consulate in South Africa and the Franco-Namibia Cultural Centre supported a production that will be showcased at the National Theatre of Namibia.
The play Little Prince in Namibia, which encompasses drama, dancing, and music, is derived from a famous French book called Le Petit Prince, translated as Little Prince.
"So it's important to develop the creative sector. But you can only develop the creative sector if people sort of know what it means. For a lot of people, art is a hobby. It's not a job. So we have to start educating people that the creative sector can actually be a job. But as with any job, be it being a doctor, being an engineer, or being a lawyer, it requires training, it requires experience, and it requires exposure. So I think it's important that we encourage young people to explore those opportunities."
The play will be showcased at NTN on the 14th and 15th of this month, and tickets are available at Web Tickets.

a3350.t:
Liberian farmers have been encouraged not to look down on themselves
By: Naneka A. Hoffman
Monrovia, Liberia, December 4, 2024 – The Executive Director of the Liberia Agency for Community Development (LACD) Mr. Adama Sarnor, encourages Liberian farmers not to view themselves as poor, emphasizing that the country’s land remains rich despite challenges they face.
Speaking in an interview, Mr. Sarnor says LACD is currently working with approximately 700 smallholder farmers and cooperatives in River Cess County, training them how to plant crops in nurseries to adapt to climate change.
He acknowledges difficulties some farmers face with this new method, as they are accustomed to traditional farming practices.
However, Mr. Sarnor assures that LACD’s experienced staff is providing necessary support to help them adjust, urging farmers to stay focused and determined.
He notes that they are key partners in Liberia’s economic development, while stressing the importance of increasing locally produced foods, particularly staples like rice, cassava, eddoes, and yam.
He highlights LACD’s role in promoting food production that addresses poverty and hunger, as well as its collaborations with international partners such as USAID, Irish Aid, Concern Worldwide, and ZOA.
He expresses gratitude for the trust these partners have placed in LACD over the years.
Mr. Sarnor calls on fellow NGO leaders in Liberia to be transparent and trustworthy, by ensuring that funds received from international donors are used appropriately for their intended purposes.
He explains that despite challenges of limited resources and heavy reliance on international aid organizations, LACD’s mission to implement sustainable programs that will improve education, livelihoods, access to services, and long-term community development is steady.
He says the vision is to ensure that every community member has the right to survival, protection, healthcare, and participation, aiming for a more sustainable and prosperous future. Editing by Jonathan Browne

Muktasari:
- Kwa jumla, kampuni hiyo imewekeza zaidi ya Sh4.5 trilioni kwenye miundombinu na huduma, huku zaidi ya Sh3 trilioni zikitumika katika kipindi cha miaka 10 iliyopita kupanua mtandao wake unaofikia zaidi ya asilimia 95 ya Watanzania.
Dar es Salaam. Katika kipindi cha miaka 25 iliyopita, Kampuni ya Vodacom Tanzania imekuwa na mchango mkubwa katika kuimarisha uchumi wa Taifa na kuinua maisha ya wananchi kupitia uwekezaji wa kihistoria, huduma za kisasa, ajira na miradi ya kijamii.
Kwa jumla, kampuni hiyo imewekeza zaidi ya Sh4.5 trilioni kwenye miundombinu na huduma, huku zaidi ya Sh3 trilioni zikitumika katika kipindi cha miaka 10 iliyopita kupanua mtandao wake unaofikia zaidi ya asilimia 95 ya Watanzania.
Kampuni hiyo inaeleza kuwa uwekezaji huu umewezesha uzinduzi wa teknolojia za kisasa kama vile 4G na 5G na kupanua upatikanaji wa intaneti ya kasi hadi kwa zaidi ya asilimia 70 ya wananchi.
Kupitia jukwaa lake la kifedha la M-Pesa, Vodacom imetambulisha huduma bunifu kama Songesha, M-Koba, malipo ya wafanyabiashara, pamoja na huduma za kijamii kama Nipige Tafu na kumgawia mwingine bando (Share the Bundle with your loved ones). Huduma hizi zimesaidia kurahisisha maisha ya Watanzania na kuwawezesha kifedha.
Kwa upande wa ajira, Vodacom imesaidia zaidi ya watu 270,000 kupata kipato kila siku kupitia ajira za moja kwa moja na zisizo za moja kwa moja, wakiwemo mawakala wa M-Pesa, wasambazaji na baadhi ya watoa huduma.
Idadi hiyo haijawaweka waajiriwa wa kampuni nyingine zinazotoa huduma kama za minara, usafi wa majengo, kampuni za magari ambazo zimepewa mikataba na Vodacom. Hilo limeongeza mchango wake katika kupunguza ukosefu wa ajira na kukuza uchumi wa ndani.
“Kwa miaka minane mfululizo, Vodacom imetambuliwa kama mwajiri bora na kwa miaka 13 hakujawahi kuripotiwa kifo cha mfanyakazi kazini,” alisema Vivienne Penessis, Mkurugenzi wa Raslimali Watu katika kampuni hiyo.
Kupitia Taasisi yake ya Vodacom Foundation, kampuni hiyo imetekeleza miradi kadhaa ya kijamii kwa ushirikiano na taasisi kama Vodafone Foundation, CCBRT, USAID na Serikali.
Miradi ya mfano ni pamoja na m-mama inayopunguza vifo vya kina mama wajawazito na watoto wachanga kwa kutoa usafiri wa dharura, pamoja na e-Fahamu, jukwaa la elimu mtandaoni linalowafikia maelfu ya wanafunzi bila gharama kwa wateja wa Vodacom. Miradi hiyo imesaidia kuboresha maisha ya zaidi ya watu milioni 10 nchini.
Kwa sasa, Vodacom inatawala soko la huduma za simu asilimia 31.9 ya wateja wote na ni miongoni mwa kampuni zilizo mstari wa mbele katika usalama wa mtandao, ikitunukiwa cheti cha kuwa "Data Processor and Controller" chini ya Sheria ya Ulinzi wa Taarifa Binafsi ya mwaka 2022.
Mafanikio haya yanatokana na uwekezaji wa kudumu katika 'mtandao, ubunifu' na teknolojia salama na kukuza vipaji vya vijana katika usalama wa mtandao hivyo kuifanya kampuni hiyo kuendelea kuwa mshirika wa maendeleo ya kiuchumi na kijamii wa Taifa.
a3369.en:
How Vodacom has injected trillions into Tanzania's economy

Summary:
- In total, the company has invested more than Sh4.5 trillion in infrastructure and services, with more than Sh3 trillion spent over the past 10 years to expand its network, which now reaches more than 95 percent of Tanzanians.

Dar es Salaam. Over the past 25 years, Vodacom Tanzania has made a major contribution to strengthening the national economy and improving citizens' lives through historic investment, modern services, employment and social projects.

In total, the company has invested more than Sh4.5 trillion in infrastructure and services, with more than Sh3 trillion spent over the past 10 years to expand its network, which now reaches more than 95 percent of Tanzanians.

The company states that this investment has enabled the launch of modern technologies such as 4G and 5G and has expanded access to high-speed internet to more than 70 percent of the population.

Through its M-Pesa financial platform, Vodacom has introduced innovative services such as Songesha, M-Koba, merchant payments, as well as social services such as Nipige Tafu and Share the Bundle with your loved ones. These services have helped make Tanzanians' lives easier and have empowered them financially.

On the employment side, Vodacom has helped more than 270,000 people earn an income every day through direct and indirect employment, including M-Pesa agents, distributors and some service providers.

That figure does not include the employees of other companies that provide services such as towers, building cleaning, and vehicle companies that have been awarded contracts by Vodacom. That has increased its contribution to reducing unemployment and growing the domestic economy.

"For eight consecutive years, Vodacom has been recognised as the best employer, and for 13 years there has never been a reported death of an employee at work," said Vivienne Penessis, the company's Director of Human Resources.

Through its Vodacom Foundation, the company has implemented several social projects in partnership with institutions such as the Vodafone Foundation, CCBRT, USAID and the Government.

Examples of these projects include m-mama, which reduces deaths of pregnant mothers and newborns by providing emergency transport, and e-Fahamu, an online education platform that reaches thousands of students free of charge for Vodacom customers. These projects have helped improve the lives of more than 10 million people in the country.

At present, Vodacom leads the mobile services market with 31.9 percent of all customers and is among the companies at the forefront of cyber security, having been awarded certification as a "Data Processor and Controller" under the Personal Data Protection Act of 2022.

These achievements stem from sustained investment in 'network, innovation' and secure technology and from developing young people's talent in cyber security, making the company continue to be a partner in the nation's economic and social development.

a3399.t:
Fineline |
Central Bank Governor Mamo Mihretu claimed a bold reconfiguration of monetary policy and foreign exchange management, marking a break from years of fiscal dominance, closed financial architecture, and constrained market signalling. He told federal legislators last week that the reforms reflect a systemic recalibration that anchors macroeconomic stability, enhances foreign exchange liquidity, and restores credibility to the central banking regime.
Over the first three quarters of the fiscal year, the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) absorbed 377.9 billion Br through 19 liquidity auctions, while the interbank market recorded 482.3 billion Br in transactions at an average interest rate of 16.8pc. Commercial banks absorbed 66.8 billion Br in treasury bonds, pushing total outstanding holdings to 161.3 billion Br, stressing the persistence of captive financing in the domestic debt market.
Governor Mamo recalled a policy rate hike to 15pc and a lending rate to 18pc, moves that not only signalled tightening to contain inflation but also heralded the end of direct monetisation of fiscal deficits. According to the Governor, the structural decoupling of central bank lending to the federal government is seen as a foundation in the central bank’s transition toward greater autonomy and inflation-targeting credibility.
Perhaps most striking was the tripling of foreign exchange reserves to cover 2.7 months of imports, a 235pc surge from the previous year, backed by strong external sector performance. The Governor projected a 2.6 billion dollar surplus in the overall balance of payments for 2024/25. Export revenues doubled to 5.3 billion dollars in Q3 alone, aided by solid returns from coffee, gold, electricity, and floriculture, while remittance inflows rose by 22pc to 5.1 billion dollars.
The capital account was buoyed by 3.8 billion dollars in receipts from foreign direct investment (FDI), public sector financing, and private loans. Official development assistance and external borrowing increased by 93pc and 77pc, respectively, partly reflecting renewed international support following policy reforms and debt restructuring agreements under the G20 Common Framework.
To counter mounting pressures from illicit capital outflows and speculative forex hoarding, the Central Bank revised its foreign exchange directive. These included caps on advance import payments, expanded allowances for travellers and businesses, and tighter margins for Forex Bureau commissions, now capped at four percent.
“We're curbing incentives for capital flight,” asserted Governor Mamo, who rejected concerns over the Bank’s profitability, arguing a 10 billion Br “unrealised loss” was due to currency depreciation, not operational mismanagement. “There is no such thing as loss. The Bank is not a profit-making institution. It pays high interest when absorbing money from the market.”
Despite booking 26 billion Br in profits, the Bank reported a net forex loss of 28.3 billion Br and raised its impairment provisions by five billion Birr, mostly for loans to state-owned enterprises according to the 2024 audit report.
Observers, such as London-based analyst Mekbib Tesfaye, have flagged the need for IFRS-compliant asset valuation and transparent reporting.
“Fair value mechanisms,” he argued, “can restore trust in central bank balance sheets.”
The Governor argued that NBE’s transformation was further reflected in structural reforms such as a revised banking proclamation that allowed foreign bank entry, the first mobile money license awarded to a foreign investor, and key institutions like the Deposit Insurance Fund and pension agencies reported digital and regulatory overhauls.
Yet, Parliament’s Budget & Finance Standing Committee, chaired by Desalegn Wedaje, raised red flags. Members of the committee criticised persistent forex crunch, the widening premium in the parallel market, unattractive deposit rates, liquidity mismatches, and operational inefficiencies in pension funds. MPs also flagged cybersecurity risks, farmers' exclusion from financial services, and pension fund inefficiencies, including low collection rates and a lack of investment planning, as critical bottlenecks.
Vice Governor Solomon Desta reiterated the NBE’s commitment to inclusive finance, citing the rollout of warehouse financing and green card services in northern regions. He disclosed that a Rural Financial Inclusion Council is also being formed.
Inflation, persistent at 14.4pc in May, with non-food prices climbing 17.8pc, fueled legislators' scepticism about Governor Mamo's bullish forecast of a decline to a single digit next year.
Economist Girum Ameha, while lauding reserve gains, warned that 2.7 months' coverage still falls short of the three-month prudential benchmark. He urged diversification beyond gold and coffee exports.
While the Bank’s position may reflect a conservative approach, it exposes a structural shortcoming. Equity investments in international financial markets offer not only diversification but also a hedge against currency depreciation. Targeted allocations in low-risk, liquid foreign assets could strengthen the Bank’s portfolio resilience.
"This is where Ethiopia can take a page from global peers," Mekbib told Fortune. "Central banks in comparable economies have leveraged equity exposure to bolster policy flexibility and manage reserve adequacy."
Experts also questioned the sustainability of foreign liabilities, such as Abu Dhabi’s deposits ballooning to 174 billion Br at a rate of four per cent interest. Projections reveal these could swell to 390 billion Br with further Birr depreciation, causing latent fiscal exposure.
Fuel subsidy removals stirred controversy, with veteran banker Ameha Tefera (PhD) labelling the decision “economic sabotage,” despite the government's push for cost-reflective pricing.
“Our dependence on imports is a huge loss," he told Fortune. "There’s a huge gap between what we import and export.”
To close this gap and boost official remittance flows, Girum recommended a combination of targeted incentives and reforming the commission structure that banks earn from facilitating remittances.
"Flat caps on commissions don’t work, banks should be rewarded for performance," he said.
Bureaucratic bottlenecks, he warned, are nudging users toward the informal market. He also weighed in on treasury bond policy, following the National Bank’s directive requiring banks to purchase government securities.
"If bonds are to fill the deficit gap, they must be priced to attract," Girum argued.
The existing bulk-purchase structure, he said, adds to investor hesitation. Still, with the advent of capital market trading, he remains optimistic.
"Wealthy investors will show up if the returns are worthwhile," he said.
Ethiopia expects to receive 750 million dollars in budgetary support from the IMF and the World Bank imminently, followed by one billion dollars next year. These inflows are tied to policy reforms, including foreign exchange liberalisation that now allows exporters and service providers to retain half of their foreign exchange earnings.
However, experts say vulnerabilities remain. Inflation control is elusive, the forex premium with the parallel market persists, and the Central Bank's 430 billion Br in sub-market loans to government agencies presents long-term fiscal risks. While the economy grew by 8.1pc this fiscal year and is projected to reach 8.4pc next year, exceeding the Sub-Saharan African average of 3.6pc, the growth masks underlying fragilities, chief among them, a shallow export base and the residual impact of monetary repression.
What emerges is a Central Bank in mid-transition. Governor Mamo is expected to strike a balance between policy orthodoxy and political economy constraints, capital account reforms and reserve management discipline, as well as monetary tightening and developmental mandates. These experts say that whether these reforms coalesce into a sustainable framework remains an open question. But for the first time in over a decade, the NBE appears to be charting its own course.

a3474.t:
Addressing the nascent computer industry in 1990, information theorist Neil Postman questioned the unspoken assumption that the capacity to process information is at the heart of society’s ills.
“If children die of starvation in Ethiopia, does it occur because of a lack of information?” he asked. “Does racism in South Africa exist because of a lack of information? If criminals roam the streets of New York City, do they do so because of a lack of information?”
Postman’s prophetic words are important to remember in the aftermath of last week’s Oval Office sitdown between President Donald Trump and President Cyril Ramaphosa and his delegation.
In that infamous meeting, South Africa’s richest man Johann Rupert pleaded the case that the country’s police stations are in desperate need of Starlink — the communication technology controlled by the world’s richest man, Elon Musk.
Rupert has rightly received acclaim for his articulation of the fact that crime is devastating to the whole nation, and not one group in particular. But this particular point is worth considering.
Crime and its causes in this country are many, varied and nuanced. To his great credit once more, Rupert used the Western Cape as an example of its complexity. So often seen by outsiders as an oasis in a broader swamp, the province’s neighbourhoods endure some of South Africa’s most brutal, seemingly interminable violence.
Such crime is not going to be solved overnight with a satellite. But would the use of Starlink — presumably as a surveillance tool — have a measurable effect?
Lacking further evidence, we are not going to dispute the possibility. What we will caution against, however, is reducing our motivations to simple narratives.
The Starlink discussion is turning all shades of ugly and threatens to be the latest issue to tear at the perpetually shaky unity of our government.
Black economic empowerment has emerged as central to the debate. Resentment towards the policy has always existed but it has bubbled closer and closer to the surface as the economy falters, and the government endures sustained attack from a superpower using propaganda to cast redress as racial persecution.
As a democracy, it is incumbent on us to continually revisit the effectiveness of our practices, but it must be done for the right reasons.
The state should consider the unintended consequences that have flowed from its policies. The country might consider that in the Oval Office, the world witnessed not only our weaknesses but our peculiar, imperfect oneness as a people and ask where we are willing to compromise and for what real gain.

a3604.t:
Tchad: Succès Masra annonce une «enquête de type international» sur la mort de l'opposant Yaya Dillo
Le Premier ministre tchadien, qui était aux États-Unis la semaine dernière et qui est actuellement de passage en France, est revenu au micro de RFI sur la mort de l'opposant Yaya Dillo décédé mercredi 28 février des suites des blessures qu’il a reçues dans l’assaut du siège de son parti et qui a également coûté la vie à quatre militaires tchadiens.
Après cet épisode qui sème le trouble et l'inquiétude dans un contexte pré-électoral, Succès Masra a assuré qu'une « enquête de type international » pour « situer les responsabilités » serait ouverte.
« Le gouvernement s'est engagé à mener une enquête de type international qui permettra de situer les responsabilités à tous les niveaux. Il y a des photos, mais il y a un film, le film des événements. Je voudrais inviter chacun à regarder le film de tous les événements », a déclaré le Premier ministre.
Lire la suite sur rfi.fr . . .
a3604.en:
Chad: Succes Masra announces an "international-type investigation" into the death of opposition leader Yaya Dillo

The Chadian Prime Minister, who was in the United States last week and is currently passing through France, spoke again on RFI's airwaves about the death of opposition leader Yaya Dillo, who died on Wednesday 28 February from the wounds he received during the assault on his party's headquarters, an attack that also cost the lives of four Chadian soldiers.

After this episode, which has sown confusion and concern in a pre-electoral context, Succes Masra assured that an "international-type investigation" to "establish responsibilities" would be opened.

"The government has committed to conducting an international-type investigation that will make it possible to establish responsibilities at all levels. There are photos, but there is also a film, the film of the events. I would like to invite everyone to watch the film of all the events," the Prime Minister declared.

Read more on rfi.fr . . .

a3620.t:
Contributing writer
MONROVIA – The National Public Health Institute of Liberia (NPHIL) under the leadership of its Director-General, Dr. Dougbeh Chris Nyan, had the honor of hosting His Excellency Mark Christopher Toner, the United States Ambassador to Liberia, on Wednesday, October 16, 2024. The visit emphasized the deepening collaboration between Liberia and the United States in enhancing public health capabilities, especially during critical times like the ongoing Mpox outbreak.
Ambassador Toner’s visit to NPHIL’s Emergency Operations Center (EDC) and the new office complex under construction was marked by insightful discussions with Dr. Nyan and senior NPHIL management. The Ambassador highlighted the importance of continued U.S.-Liberia partnership in public health, emphasizing the United States’ long-standing commitment to bolstering Liberia’s ability to detect and treat infectious diseases. Representatives from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) were also present to reaffirm support for Liberia’s public health infrastructure.
Following the visit, the U.S. Embassy in Liberia posted on its official Facebook page, expressing that “Liberia is an important global health security partner for the U.S. in West Africa.” The statement further highlighted NPHIL’s significant role since its establishment in 2016, and how the U.S. government has been a proud contributor to NPHIL’s mission of preventing infectious disease outbreaks and improving the country’s health systems.
Ambassador Toner’s visit drew widespread praise from Liberians, with social media users like Zinnah Emrys Koisee thanking the United States for its “continued support towards our health system.”
Others like Ebenezer Steve Morlia expressed confidence in Dr. Nyan’s leadership, stating that “Dr. Nyan will lead the charge and make immense impacts at NPHIL.” Watson Chelley added, “Positive work Ambassador. Liberia needs more financial support from the U.S. government. We have infrastructure, human resources, and technology challenges.”
The Ambassador’s visit coincided with NPHIL’s recent announcement of the circulation of the Monkeypox virus (Mpox) Clade-Ila in Liberia. Dr. Nyan, during a press conference at NPHIL headquarters on October 13, 2024, confirmed the presence of three new cases of Mpox, bringing the total number of cases to eleven since the virus was declared a Public Health Emergency by the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa-CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in August 2024.
“Knowledge of the Mpox Clade-Ila circulating in Liberia provides critical scientific insight on how the virus spreads and how we can enhance our diagnostics, vaccine strategy, and overall response to the outbreak,” Dr. Nyan said.
Despite the current outbreak, NPHIL continues to respond to multiple health challenges, including Lassa fever, measles, and rubella. As the National Incident Management System (IMS) mobilizes resources to coordinate the national response to the Mpox outbreak, Dr. Nyan urged the public to remain calm, practice good hygiene, and report any suspected cases to health authorities.
Dr. Dougbeh Chris Nyan, a renowned infectious disease expert and 2017 African Innovation Prize Social Impact Award winner, has been at the forefront of Liberia’s public health efforts. His extensive experience in biomedical research and his expertise in developing affordable diagnostic tools for underprivileged communities have made him a key figure in the fight against infectious diseases in Liberia and other parts of the world.
The continued support from the U.S., as reaffirmed by Ambassador Toner, is expected to further strengthen NPHIL’s capacity to address Liberia’s pressing public health challenges and contribute to preventing global public health threats.

a3647.t:
Civil society organisations (CSOs) and human right activists have said they are not shaken by United States of America President Donald Trump’s order to stop support towards reproductive health rights issues.
They have since proposed identification of sustainable ways to finance initiatives in the sector locally.
The CSOs said in Lilongwe on Friday that even without the US support, various safe abortion campaigns will proceed in the country. The US has been a major funder of the safe abortion campaign globally, including in Malawi.
Centre for Human Rights and Rehabilitation executive director Michael Kaiyatsa said while the CSO leaders and activists agree that Trump’s order will have a ripple effect, the aid freeze is an opportunity for reflection on how best they can run their campaigns without depending on US funding.
Speaking in Lilongwe on Friday during a meeting of CSOs working to advance sexual and reproductive health rights in the country, he said the aid freeze serves as a reminder of the urgent need to stand firm in their commitment to promote reproductive justice.
Said Kaiyatsa: “We are at a critical juncture where our collective action can make a difference. This meeting is not merely an exchange of information, it is a call to action.
“By sharing our insights, experiences, and strategies, we can empower one another to face opposition with confidence and creativity.”
Nyale Institute executive director Godfrey Kangaunde also acknowledged the impact of Trump’s order, saying this is a wake-up call for rights activists to rethink donor dependence.
He further said without United States Agency for International Development (USAid) funding, it means there will be limited resources available for advancing the safe abortion campaign in Malawi.
Said Kangaunde: “With the US now shifting its stance, we must ask: Can we find sustainable alternatives within Malawi and Africa? Should we let this change set us back, or can we find new, local sources of support?”
CSOs under the Coalition for Prevention of Unsafe Abortion (Copua) have been pushing for a liberalised law that would expand grounds on which women can seek safe abortion.
Proponents of safe abortion argue that with such a legal framework, Malawi would eradicate the high number of women who die due to unsafe abortion.
Gender activist Emma Kaliya, who chairs Copua, said Trump does not speak for the whole world and, therefore, sovereign States can still carry on the advocacy.
In May 2021, Parliament rejected the Termination of Pregnancy Bill which seeks to amend the Abortion Law.
Currently, the law only allows a woman to abort if there are complications that put her life in danger.
However, the Bill pushed by activists since 2015, aimed to expand legal abortion from cases where the mother’s life is at risk to include rape, incest, faetal deformity, and threats to health.

a3903.t:
As an African Christian, disdainful of years of Western pressure on African governments, including Nigeria, to repeal our laws limiting or banning LGBTQ activities, I find President Donald Trump’s words on gay marriages resonating with my Christian beliefs. I was full of joy yesterday when I viewed a video clip of him in which he declared that henceforth in the USA its citizens would only be recognized as belonging to two sexes: male and female.
I know that my sentiments in this regards are shared by many evangelical Christians across Africa, especially in Kenya, Ghana and Nigeria which have in recent years come under virtual sanctions to pressure them into creating legal space for the gay community.
I know on this matter, too, my Muslim friends share a sense of relief for Trump’s reassuring pronouncement putting an end to the multiple sex register that had evolved in recent times, opposing as they are to the LGBQT lifestyle.
I know other people who are happy. None will be happier though than President Trump’s right-hand man, the maverick billionaire, tech mogul, Elon Musk; not for religious reason but, more or less, over a family matter. Musk rues his son, Xavier’s decision to become a woman years back! Before the heart breaking decision, Xavier was his favorite son and purported heir apparent, after whom he had named his latest billion dollars media acquisition X (formerly Twitter)! The dashing young lad’s transformation into a woman had devastated the old man. Musk now hopes for his son’s return to nature. I just hope the man in him has not died (apologies to Wole Soyinka, if you get my drift!)
Howbeit, President Trump is widely popular American among the evangelical Christians mainstream in Africa! But I ask, does this Christian sentiments match with our expectations of Trump? In other words, I ask, given the sentiments and emotions, are there any evidence to suggest that in his past government or the promises made for his coming administration, Trump will be beneficial to Africa, or the African Christian community, in the challenges it faces?
The intersection of religion, politics, and international relations often reveals unexpected alliances, as seen in the case of many African evangelical Christians and their sentiments toward former 45th and now 47th U.S. President Donald Trump.
This alliance, grounded predominantly in shared cultural and moral values, demonstrates how these sentiments can become complicated when examined against the backdrop of Trump’s policies and past actions. While many African evangelicals may view Trump as a champion of their values, a more nuanced exploration reveals that these feelings may not align with a beneficial reality for the continent or its people.
The Basis for Support: Shared Values and Imagery
At the heart of the support for Trump among many African evangelical Christians is a deep resonance with his proclaimed values, but hardly nothing else. His clear stance against abortion and same-sex marriage, coupled with public expressions of faith, resonates strongly in communities where evangelical Christianity is a dominant force. For many Africans, particularly in conservative circles, Trump represents a bulwark against the perceived secularism and moral decay that the Western world embodies. They elevate his rhetoric about God, Christmas, and family values, believing he embodies their aspirations for a “Christian America.”
Moreover, Trump’s occasional linguistic nods to African nations and their cultures, even if inconsistent or superficial, serve to reinforce this connection. I recall one of his meetings with some Northern Nigerian women from the distressed Borno State, and later with Ivanka Trump playing host to two of the released kidnapped Chibok girls, Lydia Pogu and Joy Bishara. When he addresses the faith of the American populace or condemns policies they view as contrary to their beliefs, he engenders a sense of camaraderie with his African supporters. For example, his almost zero diplomatic encounter during his first meeting with President Mohammadu Buhari:
“We have had very serious problems with Christians who are being murdered in Nigeria,” Mr Trump blurted out. “We are going to be working on that problem very, very hard because we cannot allow that to happen.”
As the BBC analyst remarked, this was a strategy Trump deployed to please his persecuted audience. He wrote:
“But perhaps it should not come as any surprise. Mr Trump has always been quick to jump to the defence of Christians in conflicts such as Syria and Iraq and comments like this play well to his base among Evangelical Christians in the US.”
To be fair to him, Trump ended up selling $600 million worth of arms to Nigeria even though one wonders whether it was purely a trade transaction or an assistance in fighting insurgency and terrorism in the country. I say this because the A-29 Super Tucano fighter aircraft on which most of the money was spent never got deployed by Buhari in the fight against terrorism! When some of us asked why they we’re not being deployed to the zone of banditry and terrorism in the North West, we were told it would breach the agreed condition of sales!
The Discrepancy Between Sentiment and Policy
Politicians are all one and the same. Conversing in rhetoric is one thing and quite another to translate words into effective action; thus, the actual policies of Trump’s administration in Africa tell a different story. Despite his supporters’ hopes, Trump’s past policies often suggest a bleak outlook for Africa. His administration implemented cuts to the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), which had direct implications for development aid, health programs, and humanitarian assistance throughout the African continent. The approach towards aid and partnership during Trump’s presidency shifted to a transactional model, a sort of quid pro quo, that many argue was more about insular American interests than sustainable development in Africa.
Moreover, Trump’s harsh immigration policies and derogatory references to certain nations reinforce a narrative of neglect and disregard for African countries. His infamous “s**thole countries” remark, a blatant display of prejudice, starkly contrasts with the “Christian values” many African evangelicals see in him. Such statements create a barrier to fruitful engagement between the U.S. and African nations, disillusioning many who genuinely wish to forge stronger partnerships based on mutual growth and respect.
An Overemphasis on Personal Image Over Practical Measures
The perceived alignment of Christian values can lead to an overemphasis on personal image over practical policy; pomp and rhetoric characteristic of President Trump can obscure the tangible reality of governance. African evangelicals’ idealization of Trump often overlooks how domestic U.S. policies intersect and affect global issues. The administration’s “America First” or “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) mantra, while appealing to a nationalist agenda, raised significant concerns among African nations that depend on U.S. aid, trade, and diplomatic engagement.
Trump’s presidency in the past also saw a dip in multilateral cooperation on global challenges such as climate change, healthcare, and education, areas where African nations face existential threats. Rather than finding common ground or allyship, many African states faced unilateral withdrawal from agreements that, while seen as burdensome by some in the U.S., were lifelines for the most vulnerable populations in Africa.
Misplaced Expectations in the Second Coming of Trump
An indication that Trump’s policies have not diverted from the past is his decision to leave the World Health Organization (WHO) upon which many African countries depended on in the past to fight scourges and epidemics as small pox, polio, Ebola and Corona-19 and still do so to make live meaningful to millions on the continent. As the major financial contributor to WHO, this abandonment is tantamount to the betrayal of the people of Africa who believed in him. And this is just one of his Day One activities!
The sentiments expressed by many African evangelicals are also misguided. Given the pattern of his previous administration, it is crucial to interrogate whether economic policies or social agendas will benefit African nations. The return of Trump does not come with a guarantee of improved relations or a renewed commitment to support or uplift impoverished communities in Africa.
Furthermore, as time has progressed and the geopolitical landscape shifts, especially now that Trump’s horizon encompasses an imperialist viewpoint and globalist agenda, it’s essential for African leaders to critically assess the nature of their expectations from second term of the Trump administration. Their advocacy, in many cases rooted more in emotional appeal than in hard policy analysis, risks neglecting the very real consequences that Trump’s governance may have on the socio-economic fabrics of African nations.
Conclusion: A Call for Reflection and Reevaluation
In summary, therefore, African Christians’ sentiments for Trump shouldn’t be applied through the lens of only shared moral values and emotions, but by reach out in informed and realistic demands and expectations. Since we know his policies and rhetoric often fail to align with the needs and aspirations of African communities, we should be prepared to apply diplomatic, political and strategic pressures to be heard in Washington by Trump . Otherwise we will continue to remain irrelevant to his agenda.
In an era where many regions face challenges that transcend national boundaries, the ability to critically evaluate political alliances through a lens of pragmatism rather than sentimentality is essential. African evangelical Christians have a role to play in advocating for policies that promote genuine development and partnership with the USA.
*Dr Ishaku is Member, Editorial Advisory Board of Independent Newspapers

a3923.t:
I woke up on Thursday, May 29th, 2025, to a tribute to Ngugi wa Thiong'o, written by my California-based friend, Adeyombo Aderinto. That tribute alerted me to the passing of that giant of African writing; certainly, one of the greatest names in progressive African literature. Much later on Thursday, I also saw Okey Ndibe's short tribute and a galaxy of pictures that he had taken over the years with Ngugi. For me, Ngugi, along with the Senegalese Sembene Ousmane and the South African, Alex La Guma, represented the most radical tradition of African anti- and post-colonial writing.
As part of our study of literature in the final year of secondary school in 1976, Ngugi's WEEP NOT, CHILD, was our text for African literature. It was my introduction to the reality, as well as the deeply emotional responses, that the anti-colonial struggle in Kenya generated. That dialectical interplay would have a more profound meaning for me into the future, as I deepened my understanding of the politics of African liberation.
I went to work soon after secondary school, when I was recruited by Radio Nigeria, in 1977. I resumed work during the World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC '77). One of the highlights of FESTAC was Kenya's dramatic entry, THE TRIAL OF DEDAN KIMATHI, written by Ngugi in 1976, which was based on the anti-colonial hero, who was eventually captured and executed by British Imperialism.
Ngugi was a child of the emergency in Kenya and the anti-colonial liberation struggle that the British termed the "Mau Mau Revolt." The peasants, who were the main partisans and were led by Dedan Kimathi, knew what they were fighting for. They called themselves the Land and Freedom Army. It was a ferocious struggle that was brutally suppressed by the British and was eventually betrayed by the neocolonial elites led by Jomo Kenyatta.
It was indicative that Kenyatta was actually succeeded by Daniel Arap Moi, a home guard, who actively sided with the British during the war. Land remains central to the aspirations of the Kenyan peasantry until today. Ngugi's family was deeply affected by that brutal war, and it wasn't a surprise that most of his writings came against the backdrop of the war and the betrayal of its outcomes by the Kenyan ruling class.
Moi was to detain Ngugi for a year for his writings and suspicions about his possible activism in the underground Marxist-Leninist movement in Kenya. The symbolism of that detention couldn't have been clearer: an imperialist agent in power detained a writer whose brother fought and died in the Kenyan liberation war.
By the late 1970s, my generation had become immersed in anti-imperialist and Marxist-Leninist organizing in Nigeria and around the African continent. We were inspired by the world-wide social upheaval of the epoch. These included the armed struggle in the Portuguese colonies in Africa: Angola, Guinea-Bissau, and Mozambique. These were not just the typical anti-colonial struggles, but they were led by movements and individuals who had very clear ideas of the content of the world they were fighting for.
Similarly, there had been the epic stirring in the belly of the largest whale in the sea of human exploitation, the United States of America, with the emergence of Martin Luther King, Malcolm X, the Black Panthers and Angela Davis. Europe also saw the continent-wide students' revolts of the 1960s and these had confluenced with the huge demonstrations against the war in Vietnam, the exemplary endeavours of the Cuban Revolution and the outstanding individuals that exemplified it's impact, like Fidel Castro and Che Guevara.
Against this remarkable historical epoch and the subverted reality that became the outcome of the Kenyan struggle for independence, Ngugi's ouvre became ever more reflective of a growing consciousness in Kenya, as in much of Africa, located within the aspirations of its working people.
I think his 1977 novel, PETALS OF BLOOD, was an epic expression of the class content of the post-colonial Kenyan reality that signposted the arrival of a neocolonial bourgeoisie, entrapped in its new-fangled wealth and the bitter aftermath of the suffering for most of those who made sacrifices for the independence that hadn't satisfied their aspirations nor recognized their heroism. Africa, through the story that Ngugi masterfully told, was on the road to perdition not liberation.
The fifty years of mind conditioning to institute neoliberal capitalism have borne out the truth of Ngugi's remarkable insights. Today, Africa is a continent of very young people, with a median age in 2024 of 19.2 years. These are the children whose joyful burden would have been to build their continent, but unfortunately, the choices made by the ruling classes and the groveling toadying to imperialism, have deepened despair and a tragic desire to escape to other climes.
The prison experience took Ngugi on a radical new path of advocacy for and writing in his native language, Gikuyu. Although he had begun a process of interrogation of what he described as "the general bourgeois education system" in Kenya, before his detention, including efforts at "demystifying" theatrical performances. It was after his detention that the struggle for language and memory as a major aspect of the struggle to conclude liberation in the continent became a strident reality for Ngugi. He never abandoned that path till he breathed his last.
It was a truly revolutionary endeavor and the Kenyan neocolonial regime of Arap Moi, saw the danger that posed to the entire architecture of oppression. The dramatic work that he co-authored with Ngugi wa Mirii, Ngaahika Ndeeda (I Will Marry When I Want) was staged with peasants and working people taking active part, not just as actors, but as protagonists telling the stories of their lives. The symbolism, the consciousness raising, and the working people as makers of history became too powerful, a symbol of what neocolonial independence betrayed. The play was banned.
Not only that, his house was raided, and books were taken away. Some of the culprits carted away included Marx, Lenin, Mao, and other "subversives." All through history, reactionary regimes have either seized or burnt books!
Ngugi wa Thiong'o left a very rich collection of novels, short stories, plays, poems, essays, and also an exemplary life of commitment that would inspire future generations on our much exploited African continent. A continent that has tremendous possibilities for liberation, despite the doom and gloom of contemporary existence. It was that hope for the better which ran through the works and life of one of our greatest writes, Ngugi wa Thiong'o.
A lot went on tragically in his personal life including the gang rape of his wife in order to humiliate him, his forced self-exile, and the loneliness of old age far away from the Kenya and Africa that he loved with tremendous passion. As Fredrich Engels said in his funeral oration for Karl Marx, mankind was a head shorter with his passing, and no doubts for us in Africa, we have indeed lost one of our greatest heads!
*Is'haq Modibbo Kawu, PhD, FNGE, is a Broadcaster, Journalist and Political Scientist.*

a4044.t:
Russia has been unable to send aid to Africa due to sanctions, the Foreign Ministry said.
MOSCOW, February 20 – RIA Novosti. Due to sanctions, Russia was unable to send money for food aid to African countries such as Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger and Sudan in 2024, Tatyana Dovgalenko, head of the Department for Partnership with Africa at the Russian Foreign Ministry, said in an interview with RIA Novosti.
According to her, Russia provides humanitarian assistance to African countries in need both through bilateral channels and through international organizations, including through the United Nations World Food Program (WFP). According to Dovgalenko, it is a key multilateral channel for Moscow to provide such assistance.
"The Government of the Russian Federation has allocated the necessary financing to the program for the supply of domestic food to Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger and Sudan. However, due to the sanctions imposed by Washington in November 2024 against Russian financial institutions, including those that serve our donor projects in international organizations, it has not yet been possible to transfer funds," Dovgalenko said.
She recalled that Russia has been sending an annual contribution of $10 million to WFP since 2020, and last year was no exception.
"This situation clearly illustrates the falsity of Western statements about the so-called "humanitarian exemptions" and the "targeted" nature of illegal unilateral restrictions against Russia," the diplomat added.
She stressed that Moscow is taking steps to find a solution to these problems, and as soon as the issue of transferring Russian donor funds is resolved, the WFP will coordinate with the national governments of the beneficiary countries the nomenclature of the necessary food, and suppliers will satisfy these requests.
